966769.title: Wellington, Shropshire
966769.extract: Wellington is a market town and a civil parish in the borough of Telford and Wrekin, Shropshire, England. It is situated 3 miles (4.8 km) north-west of Telford and 12 miles (19 km) east of Shrewsbury, near the western terminus of the M54 motorway. The summit of The Wrekin lies 3 miles to the south-west. Wellington’s population was 25,554 in the 2011 census.

main.*: {{Short description|Market town in Shropshire, England}} {{Use British English|date=October 2013}} {{Use dmy dates|date=July 2024}} {{More citations needed|date=February 2018}} {{Infobox UK place |country = England |coordinates = {{coord|52.7001|-2.5157|display=inline,title}} |official_name= Wellington |population = 25,554 |civil_parish = Wellington |unitary_england= [[Telford and Wrekin]] |lieutenancy_england= [[Shropshire]] |region= West Midlands |constituency_westminster= [[The Wrekin (UK Parliament constituency)|The Wrekin]] |post_town= TELFORD |postcode_district = TF1 |postcode_area= TF |dial_code= 01952 |os_grid_reference= SJ651115 | static_image_name = {{multiple images |perrow=1 2 2 1|total_width=250px|align=center | image1 = Wellington Market Street - geograph.org.uk - 7018233.jpg | image2 = The Parish Church of All Saints, Wellington - geograph.org.uk - 7018246.jpg | image3 = Sunnycroft Wellington - geograph.org.uk - 2513733.jpg | image4 = Wellington, Telford Central Mosque - geograph.org.uk - 4978184.jpg | image5 = Wellington, Wrekin Buildings - geograph.org.uk - 4979532.jpg }} | static_image_caption = Clockwise from the top: Wellington Market Street, [[Sunnycroft]], Wrekin Buildings, [[Telford Central Mosque|Central Mosque]] and [[All Saints Church, Wellington|All Saints Church]] | website = {{URL|https://www.wellington-shropshire.gov.uk/}} |static_image_2_name= Wellington arms.png |static_image_2_width= 125px |static_image_2_caption=Parish coat of arms | parts_type = Areas of the town | p1 = [[Admaston, Shropshire|Admaston]] | p2 = Arleston | p3 = [[Bratton, Shropshire|Bratton]] | p4 = [[Dothill]] | p5 = Ercall | type = Town and civil parish }} '''Wellington''' is a [[market town]] and a [[civil parish]] in the borough of [[Telford and Wrekin]], [[Shropshire]], England. It is situated {{convert|3|mi}} north-west of [[Telford]] and {{convert|12|mi}} east of [[Shrewsbury]], near the western terminus of the [[M54 motorway]]. The summit of [[The Wrekin]] lies 3 miles to the south-west. Wellington’s population was 25,554 in the [[2011 United Kingdom Census|2011 census]]. ==History== [[File:AllSaintsWellington.JPG|thumb|right|All Saints' Church in the centre of Wellington, built in 1789]] The origin of the name ''Wellington'' is the subject of debate. One theory derives it from the [[Old English]] ''weolaingtūn'' meaning 'settlement connected with Weola'. Other theories derive it from ''waluingtūn'' meaning 'settlement at the walled place' or ''wēohlēahtūn'' meaning 'holy settlement in a wood or clearing'. Alternatively, the first element could be ''wēoling'' meaning 'mechanical device'.{{cite web |url=http://kepn.nottingham.ac.uk/map/place/Shropshire/Wellington |title=Key to English place-names |work=University of Nottingham |access-date=20 December 2025}} A church has stood for almost 1,000{{nbsp}}years and a priest is mentioned in the [[Domesday Book]]. The original churchyard still remains. [[All Saints Church, Wellington|All Saints Church]] was designed by [[George Steuart (architect)|George Steuart]] and was built in 1789.{{cite web|url=http://www.allsaints-wellington.org/|title=All Saints, Wellington|website=All Saints, Wellington|access-date=10 April 2018|archive-date=13 December 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231213072901/http://allsaints-wellington.org/|url-status=dead}} Wellington's first market charter was granted to Giles of Erdington, lord of the manor, in 1244 and a market still exists today.{{Citation needed|date=April 2022}} The market had an open-sided market hall by 1680, and possibly much earlier, but it was dismantled in about 1805.{{Citation needed|date=April 2022}} In 1841 a market company was formed to purchase the market rights from [[John George Weld Weld-Forester, 2nd Baron Forester|Lord Forester]] in 1856."Wellington: Economic History", in ''A History of the County of Shropshire: Volume 11: Telford'' (1985), pp. 222–232. [http://www.british-history.ac.uk/report.aspx?compid=18142&strquery=Wellington, Shropshire market]. Date accessed: 20 May 2008. In 1848, the company built a town hall with the butter market below, creating a permanent covered space for traders. The first Shropshire Olympian Games, organised by celebrated Olympic revivalist Dr [[William Penny Brookes]], were held in Wellington in May 1861.{{cite book|last=Beale|first=Catherine|title=Born out of Wenlock, William Penny Brookes and the British origins of the modern Olympics|year=2011|publisher=D.B. Publications, Derby|page=52|isbn=978-1-85983-967-6}} In August 1868, the town hosted the third National Olympian Games, organised by the [[British Olympic Association|National Olympian Association]] co-founded by Brookes, when their intended venue at [[Manchester]] had become unavailable.''Born out of Wenlock, William Penny Brookes and the British origins of the modern Olympics'', p.73. To the north-east of the town is the site of [[Apley Castle]], originally a 14th-century fortified manor house; the remains were converted into a stable block with the building of a grand Georgian house, which was itself demolished in 1955.{{cite book|last=Emery|first=Anthony|year=2000 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FRw9AAAAIAAJ |title=Greater Medieval Houses of England and Wales, 1300-1500: East Anglia, Central England and Wales |pages=607–8|publisher=Cambridge: Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-58131-8}} The surviving stable block has been converted into apartments and retains some medieval features.{{cite PastScape|mnumber=72267 |mname=Apley Castle|access-date=26 February 2014}} ===The creation of Telford=== [[File:TelfordMap.jpg|thumb|right|A map of Telford; Wellington is shown in magenta]] Dawley New Town was designated by the government in 1963 and was expanded to encompass Wellington in 1968; it was given the new name of [[Telford]], after the great engineer and first [[county surveyor]] of Shropshire, [[Thomas Telford]]. The creation of Telford has divided opinion in Wellington ever since, with some celebrating the jobs and investment it brought to the area and others bemoaning the negative impact on Wellington's own economy; as well as its status and sense of identity.{{cite web|url=http://www.british-history.ac.uk/report.aspx?compid=18062|title=Telford |website=British History on-line |access-date=10 April 2018}} The development of [[Telford Town Centre]] and local retail parks since the 1970s had an adverse effect on Wellington's retail centre.{{cn|date=June 2025}} The local [[association football|football]] team's name was changed from Wellington Town to [[Telford United F.C.|Telford United]] in 1969.{{fchd|id=TELFORDU|name=Telford United}} For many years, local politics left Wellington in conflict with Wrekin District (now [[Telford and Wrekin Council]]), with claims and counterclaims of neglect. In the 21st century, however, the borough council has invested heavily in the town. These investments include the redeveloped Wellington Civic and Leisure Centre, near the centre of the town, which has brought together the library, town council, swimming pool and gym, along with a modern [[Register office (United Kingdom)|register office]]. Two hundred borough council officers are also located at the new complex.{{citation needed|date=March 2022}} ==Commerce== The area's largest employers are located in nearby areas of Telford, with Wellington itself housing hundreds of small businesses in its shops, offices and small manufacturing units. A range of nationwide chains have branches in Wellington; the [[Wrekin Retail Park]] is located in the town. ==Attractions== [[The Wrekin]], one of Shropshire's most famous landmarks, is the most northern part of the [[Shropshire Hills AONB|Shropshire Hills Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty]]. Located just {{convert|2.5|mi}} from the centre of Wellington, it attracts tens of thousands of walkers and cyclists to the town every year.{{cite web|url=https://www.shropshirestar.com/entertainment/attractions/2019/07/08/plan-to-protect-and-enhance-wrekin-forest/|title=Plan to protect and enhance Wrekin forest|date=8 July 2019|access-date=2 November 2019|via=shropshirestar.com}} Located in the town's Victorian market hall, Wellington Market operates four days a week and houses over 50 stalls. A short walk from the centre of the town is [[Sunnycroft]], a Victorian villa and mini-estate now owned and run by the [[National Trust]].{{cite web |title=Sunnycroft |access-date =7 July 2025 |url=https://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/place/sunnycroft |publisher=National Trust}} The town is home to the Belfrey Theatre, an amateur venue run by the Wellington Theatre Company, which offers an annual season of plays and other shows. ==Transport== [[File:Wellington Railway Station -Shropshire-27Jan2008.jpg|thumb|right|Wellington railway station]] Wellington has road links, centrally located railway and bus stations, and a position on routes 45 and 81 of the National Cycle Network. === Railway === [[Wellington railway station (Shropshire)|Wellington railway station]] is served by two [[train operating companies]]: * [[Transport for Wales Rail|Transport for Wales]] operates hourly services between {{rws|Birmingham International}} and West Wales; destinations alternate between {{rws|Aberystwyth}} and {{rws|Pwllheli}}, and {{rws|Holyhead}}{{Cite web |title=Timetables |work=Transport for Wales |date=10 December 2023 |access-date=12 April 2024 |url=https://tfw.wales/service-status/timetables}} * [[West Midlands Trains]] operates hourly services each way between {{rws|Shrewsbury}} and {{rws|Birmingham New Street}}, via {{rws|Wolverhampton}}.{{Cite web |title=Train timetables and schedules |work=West Midlands Railway |date=10 December 2023 |access-date=12 April 2024 |url= https://www.westmidlandsrailway.co.uk/travel-information/journey-planning/timetables}} ====History==== The station was built in 1849. In 1867, a branch line was opened to connect the town with [[Market Drayton]]. The [[Wellington and Market Drayton Railway]] operated for almost a hundred years before closure under the [[Beeching Axe]] in 1963. The line remained open for goods only services until 1967; the track was lifted in 1970.{{cite book |last=Yate |first=Bob |title=By Great Western to Crewe |publisher=The Oakwood Press |date=2005 |location=Usk |isbn=0-85361-639-6}}{{cite book |last=Lester |first=C.R. |title=The Stoke to Market Drayton Line |publisher=The Oakwood Press |date=1983 |location=Usk |isbn=0-85361-293-5}} There were also railway links to {{rws|Much Wenlock}}, closed in 1962, and {{rws|Stafford}}, which closed in the late 1960s. A goods only link to a [[Telford International Railfreight Park|rail head at Donnington]], on part of the former Wellington to Stafford line, has been reopened.{{cite web|title=New operator for Telford International Railfreight Park|url=http://www.telford.gov.uk/news/article/833/new_operator_for_telford_international_railfreight_park|website=Telford.gov.uk|accessdate=28 January 2016|date=2 July 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160131113750/http://www.telford.gov.uk/news/article/833/new_operator_for_telford_international_railfreight_park|archive-date=31 January 2016|url-status=dead|df=dmy-all}} There have been campaigns to reopen the whole of the line from Shrewsbury to Stafford through Wellington, Leegomery, [[Hadley, Shropshire|Hadley]], [[Trench, Telford|Trench]], [[Donnington, Telford|Donnington]] and [[Newport, Shropshire|Newport]].{{cite web|url=https://www.shropshirestar.com/news/transport/2017/01/10/petition-calls-for-reopening-of-shrewsbury-to-stafford-railway-line/|title=Petition calls for reopening of Shrewsbury to Stafford railway line|website=shropshirestar.com|access-date=10 April 2018}} === Buses === [[File:New Bus Station, Wellington - geograph.org.uk - 1383423.jpg|thumb|Wellington bus station, prior to its redesign in 2022]] Current bus services operated by [[Arriva Midlands]] in Wellington are:{{Cite web |title=Wellington bus services |work=Bus Times |date=2024 |access-date=12 April 2024 |url= https://bustimes.org/localities/wellington-telford}} * 4: [[Madeley, Shropshire|Madeley]] – Leegomery * 7: Wellington – [[Telford Centre]] * X7: Telford Centre – Shrewsbury * 8: Telford/Wellington – [[Bridgnorth]] * X10A: Telford Centre – Shrewsbury * 99 – Telford circular. In late 2022, Telford and Wrekin Council introduced the ''Travel Telford'' services, operated by [[Chaserider]] and Select Bus Services; these are: * 100: Wellington – Sutton Hill * 101: Madeley – Princess Royal Hospital * 102/3: Wellington – [[Newport, Shropshire|Newport]]. ====History==== After World War I, [[BMMO]] expanded its depots out from [[Birmingham]] to other towns and cities in the [[Midlands]], including Shrewsbury.[https://web.archive.org/web/20081011064332/http://madeinbirmingham.org/midlandred.htm Birmingham and Midland Motor Omnibus Company (Midland Red)] Made in Birmingham Thus would later lead to them opening a depot on Charlton Street on 21 July 1932, after closing the Shrewsbury depot in the same month.{{cn|date=February 2026}} BMMO was later renamed to Midland Red Omnibus Company in March 1974 and was split up in September 1981 to become Midland Red (North) Limited, with whom the depot was taken control of. Midland Red North was later acquired by the Cowie Group on 1 August 1996, which would rename it to become Arriva on 6 November 1997. After 80 years of the Charlton Street depot being in operation, it would be closed by Arriva in April 2012 and demolished in summer of 2015. The fleet and staff from the depot were moved to a new premises on Stafford Park prior to its demolition. ==Events== The area's music and theatre groups host performances throughout the year, and there are craft markets at both Belmont Hall and Christ Church. In March, the town marks ''Charter Day'', when the 1244 charter is delivered by a messenger on horseback. A jury then convenes in the Market Square to appoint the town crier, ale taster and market clerk for the year ahead. During the summer, around 40 events take place in and around the town; these include the historically inspired Midsummer Fayre, the town carnival and Lions Day at Bowring Park, and the Wellington Walking Festival. ''Sounds in The Square'' brings live music to the heart of the town across weekends in July and August, and various concerts and fetes complete the programme. The Wellington Arts Festival runs every October and offers a variety of events including plays, music, exhibitions, literature and poetry. ==Education and health services== Wellington is the main education centre for the borough. Telford College and the independent school [[Wrekin College]] are located around the outskirts of the town, along with several primary and secondary schools. The [[Princess Royal Hospital, Telford|Princess Royal Hospital]], one of Shropshire's two main hospitals, is located just outside the town at [[Apley Castle|Apley]], as is the Severn Hospice. Within the town, Wellington Health Centre is the main GP practice. The former [[cottage hospital]] was endowed in 1910 by Ann Bowring, in memory of her husband John, a successful fish merchant and railway entrepreneur. The hospital, which opened on the Haygate Road in 1913, was used as a military auxiliary hospital during World War I. Threatened with closure in 1919, it was saved by local fundraising and continued to serve as a local hospital and later a care home, under the regional Health Board.{{cite web |title=Wellington Cottage Hospital |url=https://www.wellingtonswar.co.uk/the-heritage/wellington-cottage-hospital/ |website=Wellington's War |access-date=6 January 2025}}{{cite web |title=Wellington: Public services A History of the County of Shropshire: Volume 11, Telford |url=https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/salop/vol11/pp236-238 |website=British History Online |publisher=Victoria County History, 1985 |access-date=6 January 2025}} ==Media== Local news and television programmes are provided by [[BBC West Midlands]] and [[ITV Central]]. Television signals are received from the [[The Wrekin transmitting station|Wrekin]] TV transmitter.{{cite web|url=https://ukfree.tv/transmitters/tv/The_Wrekin|title=Full Freeview on the The[sic] Wrekin (Telford and Wrekin, England) transmitter|date=1 May 2004|website=UK Free TV|access-date=20 July 2024}} Local radio stations are [[BBC Radio Shropshire]], [[Hits Radio Black Country & Shropshire]], [[Greatest Hits Radio Black Country & Shropshire]] and [[Capital North West and Wales]]. The town is served by local newspaper, [[Shropshire Star]].{{Cite web |url=https://www.shropshirestar.com/ |title=Shropshire Star |access-date=20 July 2024}} ==Community projects== A number of community organisations are active in the town, including the ''Walkers are Welcome'' group and ''Wellington H2A'', which promotes arts and heritage in the town through a range of events. Local history and heritage are promoted by Wellington History Group and the Civic Society. Amongst current community projects are the Peace Garden,{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-shropshire-17189215|title=Civic centre peace garden plans|publisher=BBC News |date=28 February 2012|access-date=10 April 2018}} started by local nonagenarian George Evans (died 2020), and the ambitious project to return a cinema to the town for the first time since the closure of the Clifton almost three decades ago. In June 2019, the ''Wellington Orbit'' was opened, bringing a cafe, bar and cinema to the centre of the town; it is operated by a team of volunteers.{{cite web |url=https://www.shropshirestar.com/entertainment/telford-entertainment/2019/06/28/lights-camera-action-as-wellingtons-new-cinema-to-show-its-first-film |title='Lights, camera, action' as Wellington's new cinema to show its first film |date=28 June 2019 |access-date=2 November 2019 |website=Shropshirestar.com}}{{cite web |url=https://wellingtonorbit.co.uk/ |title=Wellington Orbit |website=Wellingtonorbit.co.uk}} ==Sport== The New Buck's Head football stadium, home to [[AFC Telford United]], is in Wellington. Other sporting clubs include the [[Wellington Cricket Club]], currently in the Birmingham League Premier Division, and Wrekin Golf Club. ==Twin towns== Wellington is [[sister city|twinned]] with [[Châtenay-Malabry]], France. A twinning group exists to maintain links with the town.[http://wellington-twinning.co.uk/ Wellington Shropshire twinning association] retrieved 21 January 2019 ==Notable people== {{main category|People from Wellington, Shropshire}} The town's literary claims to fame include it being the birthplace of 19th-century evangelical religious writer [[Hesba Stretton]] (1832–1911), and the first job of poet [[Philip Larkin]] (1922–1985) was as librarian of Wellington Library from 1943 to 1946. Larkin described Wellington as a "hole full of toad's turds" and stated that his job as town librarian was to "hand out tripey novels to morons".{{cite news|url=http://www.shropshirestar.com/news/2011/04/02/letter-what-did-philip-larkin-ever-do-for-wellington|title=Letter: What did Philip Larkin ever do for Wellington?|newspaper=Shropshire Star|access-date=12 April 2012}} A walkway at the side of Wellington Library was named Larkin Way in honour of Philip Larkin, but this pathway was lost during redevelopment work on the library. Larkin Way, in a slightly modified form, still exists. The Wellington Civic and Leisure Centre is on Larkin Way.{{cite web |url=https://livewell.telford.gov.uk/Services/815 |title = Wellington Civic & Leisure Centre {{!}} Live Well Telford}} Reverend [[Patrick Brontë]] (1777–1861) lived in the town for a year while serving a curacy before moving to Yorkshire and meeting his future wife there, [[Maria Branwell]] (1783–1821), with whom he had four notable Brontë children. The abolitionist Dr [[William Withering]] (1741–1799) was born in the town; he investigated [[digitalis]], used in the treatment of [[heart disease]]. Several members of the pop group [[T'Pau (band)|T'Pau]] (active 1986–1992), including vocalist [[Carol Decker]] (born 1957) and keyboardist Michael Chetwood, grew up in Wellington; the latter returning to run a music shop in the town. 1094553.title: Brean Down Fort
1094553.extract:
Brean Down Fort was a Victorian naval fortification designed to protect the Bristol Channel. It was built 60 feet (18 m) above sea level on the headland at Brean Down, 9 miles (14 km) south of Weston-super-Mare, Somerset, England.
The site has a long history because of its prominent position. The earliest recorded settlement is from the Early to Middle Bronze Age.
The current buildings were constructed in the 1860s as one of the Palmerston Forts to provide protection to the ports of the Bristol Channel, and was decommissioned in 1901. During World War II it was rearmed and used for experimental weapons testing.
The site has been owned by the National Trust since 2002, following a £431,000 renovation project, as part of its Brean Down property and is open to the public.

{{Short description|19th-century military fortification in Somerset, England}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2020}} {{Infobox military installation |name=Brean Down Fort |partof= |location=[[Somerset]], [[England]] |coordinates={{Coord|51|19|38.03|N|3|02|00.08|W |type:landmark_region:GB_scale:10000|display=inline,title }} |image=Breandownfort.JPG |image_size=240px |caption= |image2= |caption2= |map_type=Somerset |type= |code= |built= 1864–1871
rearmed in [[World War II]] |builder= |materials= |height= |used=1871–1901, 1940–1945 |demolished= |condition= |ownership=[[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] |open_to_public=The site remains unlocked at all times, with volunteers manning buildings on summer weekends and Mon, Wed, Fri in summer school holidays |controlledby= |garrison=Coast Brigade, [[Royal Artillery]] |current_commander= |commanders= |occupants= |battles= |events= }} '''Brean Down Fort''' was a Victorian naval fortification designed to protect the [[Bristol Channel]]. It was built {{convert|60|ft|m|0}} above sea level on the headland at [[Brean Down]], {{convert|9|mi|km|0}} south of [[Weston-super-Mare]], [[Somerset]], England. The site has a long history because of its prominent position. The earliest recorded settlement is from the Early to Middle [[Bronze Age]]. The current buildings were constructed in the 1860s as one of the [[Palmerston Forts]] to provide protection to the ports of the Bristol Channel, and was decommissioned in 1901. During [[World War II]] it was rearmed and used for experimental weapons testing. The site has been owned by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] since 2002, following a £431,000 renovation project,{{cite web|url=http://archive.thisisthewestcountry.co.uk/2002/6/27/37692.html |title=Historic Brean Down Fort re-opens after £431,000 renovation |date=27 June 2002 |work=This is the West County |access-date=6 May 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080511192355/http://archive.thisisthewestcountry.co.uk/2002/6/27/37692.html |archive-date=11 May 2008 }} as part of its Brean Down property and is open to the public. The fort was used as a location for filming of the second episode, "Warriors", of the [[BBC]] television drama ''[[Bonekickers]]''. The fort was also used for exterior scenes of the [[Royal Marines]] attack on the villains base on Cragfest Island in episode six of 1978 [[ITV Wales & West|HTV]] series ''[[The Doombolt Chase]]''. ==Bronze Age to Roman== The earliest record settlement is from the Early to Middle [[Bronze Age]]. It is now on an exposed cliff as the land has been eroded by the sea. Bronze Age artefacts from the site include pottery and jewellery. Most of the finds are now in the [[Museum of Somerset]] in [[Taunton]].{{cite web|title=Brean Down |url=http://www.pastscape.org.uk/hob.aspx?hob_id=191314 |work=National Monuments Record |publisher=[[English Heritage]] |access-date=21 March 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121002080743/http://www.pastscape.org.uk/hob.aspx?hob_id=191314 |archive-date= 2 October 2012 }} The presence of a probable roundhouse has also been detected.{{cite web|title=Brean Down|url=https://www.pastscape.org.uk/hob.aspx?hob_id=617234|work=National Monuments Record|publisher=[[English Heritage]]|access-date=21 March 2011}} The site has also produced Roman gold and silver coins of the emperors [[Augustus]], [[Nero]], [[Nero Claudius Drusus|Drusus]] and [[Vespasian]] and a cornelian ring.{{cite web|title=Hillfort, Brean Down|url=http://www.somersetheritage.org.uk/record/10115|work=Somerset Historic Environment Record|publisher=South West Heritage Trust|access-date=21 March 2011}} ==Palmerston Fort== Brean Down Fort forms part of a [[Palmerston Forts, Bristol Channel|line of defences]], known as [[Palmerston Forts]], built across the channel to protect the approaches to [[Bristol]] and [[Cardiff]]. It was fortified following a visit by [[Queen Victoria]] and [[Albert, Prince Consort|Prince Albert]] to [[France]], where they had been concerned at the strength of the French Navy. The [[Royal Commission on the Defence of the United Kingdom]], under direction of [[Lord Palmerston]], recommended fortification of the coast. Brean Down Fort formed part of a strategic coastal defence system covering the channel between the mainland and the islands of [[Steep Holm]] and [[Flat Holm]].{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}} Four acres of land at the end of Brean Down were requisitioned in 1862,{{cite web |url=http://www.somersetheritage.org.uk/record/10128 |title=Victorian artillery battery, Brean Down |work=Somerset Historic Environment Record |publisher=South West Heritage Trust |access-date=6 May 2008}} with construction beginning in 1864 and completed in 1871. The fort was originally armed with seven [[RML 7 inch 7 ton gun|{{convert|7|in|cm|0|adj=on}} rifled muzzle-loading guns]], which were among the last of this type to be made at the [[Royal Arsenal|Woolwich Gun Foundry]]. These sited at three main gun positions, including W battery containing two guns on 'C' pivots (rotating around a reused Georgian cannon set upright in the ground). Each gun weighed 7 tons and had a {{convert|30|lb|kg|0|adj=on}} charge of gunpowder able to fire a {{convert|112|lb|kg|0|adj=on}} Palliser shot at {{convert|1560|ft|m|0}} per second. This could pierce {{convert|8|in|cm|0}} of armour at {{convert|1000|yd|m}}.{{cite web |url=http://www.burnham-on-sea.com/breandown.shtml |title=A look at Brean Down's historic background |work=Burnham on Sea |access-date=6 May 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080511194720/http://burnham-on-sea.com/breandown.shtml |archive-date=11 May 2008 |url-status=dead }} It was proposed to replace the {{convert|7|in|cm|0|adj=on}} guns with larger {{convert|9|in|cm|0|adj=on}} versions in 1888 but this was never put into action. It had a large, underground, main gunpowder magazine, {{convert|15|by|18|ft|m}} and {{convert|20|ft|m}} high. The fort was staffed by 50 officers and men of the Coast Brigade, [[Royal Artillery]], but no shots were ever fired in action.{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}} In 1897, following wireless transmissions from [[Lavernock Point]] in Wales and Flat Holm,{{cite web |url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/wales/southeast/sites/flatholm/pages/marconi.shtml |title=Marconi: Radio Pioneer |access-date=12 April 2008 |work=BBC South East Wales |archive-date=22 July 2012 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120722102254/http://www.bbc.co.uk/wales/southeast/sites/flatholm/pages/marconi.shtml |url-status=dead }} [[Guglielmo Marconi]] moved his equipment to Brean Down and set a new distance record of {{convert|14|km}} for wireless transmission over open sea.{{cite web |title=Marconi at Brean Down (near Bristol) |url=http://g4usb.net/IMD/station-histories/brean-down-gb6md/ |publisher=International Marconi Day |access-date=6 February 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140219151408/http://g4usb.net/IMD/station-histories/brean-down-gb6md/# |archive-date=19 February 2014}}{{cite book|last=Garratt|first=G.R.M.|title=The Early History of Radio: From Faraday to Marconi|year=1994|publisher=IET|isbn=978-0-85296-845-1|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vd90yIE2Ya8C&q=marconi+lavernock+Brean+Down&pg=PA86}} The end of the fort's active service came at 5 a.m. on 6 July 1900 when the No. 3 magazine which held 3 tons (3 tonnes) of gunpowder exploded.van der Bijl, Nicholas [[British Empire Medal|BEM]] (2000). ''Brean Down Fort: Its History and the Defence of the Bristol Channel''. Cossington: Hawk Editions. {{ISBN|0-9529081-7-4}}. pages 71-75 An inquiry found that Gunner Haines had fired a [[Cartridge (firearm)|ball cartridge]] down a ventilator shaft causing the explosion, after being put on a charge for returning late to barracks, however this explanation has been challenged.{{cite book|last=Evans|first=Roger|title=Somerset tales of mystery and murder|date=October 2004 |publisher=Countryside Books|location=Newbury|isbn=1-85306-863-2|pages=5–11}} The wall separating the fort from the moat on the south west corner was demolished and wreckage thrown up to {{convert|200|yd|m|0}}. No one knew why the gunner had blown up the fort, but it has been speculated that it was an act of suicide. The cannons were hauled away by [[traction engine]]s. It was then used as a café, owned by the Hillman family from at least 1907 until sold in 1936 to the 'bird sanctuary people'.{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}} ==World War II== On the outbreak of [[World War II]] the fort was rearmed with two [[BL 6 inch Mk VII naval gun|six-inch]] ex-naval guns and two searchlights as a [[Coastal artillery]] battery. The site was also used as a test launch site for rockets and experimental weapons.{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}} Two gun positions were built to mount the ex-naval guns in their turrets. These were later protected with a "plastic" anti-aircraft roof. One position was built over the ruins of the old west battery and the other partly obscures the north west battery. The barrack blocks were converted and the windows partly blocked to reduce the effects of blast. Several other associated structures, including [[searchlight]] batteries for illuminating seaborne targets, a command post and the barracks for the garrison were built outside the original Palmeston fort. The site was manned by 365 and 366 Coast Batteries of [[571st Coast Regiment, Royal Artillery]], formed from Brean Down Fire Control in December 1941 and disbanded in April 1944.{{cite web |url=http://www.somersetheritage.org.uk/record/12359 |title=Second-World-War Coast Artillery battery, Brean Down |work=Somerset Historic Environment Record |publisher=South West Heritage Trust |access-date=6 May 2008}}[https://web.archive.org/web/20081123123232/http://www.ra39-45.pwp.blueyonder.co.uk/coast/page88.html 571 Coast Rgt at Royal Artillery 1939–1945.]Gen Sir [[Martin Farndale]], ''History of the Royal Regiment of Artillery: The Years of Defeat: Europe and North Africa, 1939–1941'', Woolwich: Royal Artillery Institution, 1988/London: Brasseys, 1996, {{ISBN|1-85753-080-2}}, Annexes H and M. Several experimental weapons were trialled at Brean, by the [[British Admiralty|Admiralty]]'s [[Directorate of Miscellaneous Weapons Development]], based at [[HMS Birnbeck]].{{cite web|url=http://www.birnbeckpier.org/birnbeck_pier_history.php |work=Friends of the Old Pier Society |title=Birnbeck Island Pier — A short history |access-date=6 June 2007 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928010805/http://www.birnbeckpier.org/birnbeck_pier_history.php |archive-date=28 September 2007 }} The only evidence being a short length of launching rail,{{cite web |url=http://www.somersetheritage.org.uk/record/12491 |title=Experimental weapon rails, Brean Down |work=Somerset Historic Environment Record |publisher=South West Heritage Trust |access-date=6 May 2008}} designed to launch a bouncing bomb. Some of the better known weapons trialled were the seaborne [[Bouncing bomb]] designed specifically to bounce to a target such as across water to avoid [[torpedo net]]s, [[anti-submarine missile]] AMUCK and the expendable [[sonar decoy|acoustic emitter]] (designed to confuse [[homing torpedo|noise-seeking torpedo]]es).{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}} ==Gallery== Image:Breandownfortfromnorth.JPG|The fort seen from the north path Image:Breandownfortofficersquarters.JPG|Officers quarters Image:Breandownfortgunemplacement.JPG|Gun emplacement Image:Breandownfortenginehouse.JPG|Engine House Image:Breandownfortfromsouthpath.JPG|The fort from the south path ==See also== *[[List of hillforts and ancient settlements in Somerset]] ==References== ; Notes {{reflist}} ; Sources *{{cite book|first=Ian V|last=Hogg|title=Coast Defences of England and Wales 1856-1956|publisher=David & Charles|year=1974|isbn=0-7153 6353-0}} * van der Bijl, Nicholas (2000). 1334006.title: Wenlock Edge
1334006.extract:
Wenlock Edge is a limestone escarpment near Much Wenlock, Shropshire, England and a site of special scientific interest because of its geology. It is over 19 miles (31 km) long, running southwest to northeast between Craven Arms and Much Wenlock, and is roughly 1,083 feet above sea level. The deciduous woodland which runs along it covers much of the steep slopes of the escarpment and in parts it is very well preserved.

It was featured on the 2005 TV programme Seven Natural Wonders as one of the wonders of the Midlands.
Wenlock Edge contains many interesting features such as Flounders' Folly, Wilderhope Manor and Shipton Hall and waymarked walks such as the Shropshire Way and bridleways such as the Jack Mytton Way. It is a popular area for hillwalking, cycling, mountain biking and horseriding and is also frequented by tourists and sightseers.
Robert Hart created a model forest garden from a small orchard on his farm called Highwood Hill in Wenlock Edge.

{{short description|Limestone escarpment near Much Wenlock, Shropshire, England}} {{for|the song cycle by Ralph Vaughan Williams|On Wenlock Edge (song cycle)}} {{EngvarB|date=October 2013}} {{Use dmy dates|date=July 2024}} '''Wenlock Edge''' is a [[limestone]] [[escarpment]] near [[Much Wenlock]], Shropshire, England and a [[site of special scientific interest]] because of its geology. It is over {{convert|19|mi|km}} long, running southwest to northeast between [[Craven Arms]] and Much Wenlock,{{cite web|url=http://www.naturalengland.org.uk/ourwork/conservation/geodiversity/englands/sites/local_ID76.aspx|work=Natural England|title=Wenlock Edge (SSSI)|access-date=29 June 2013}} and is roughly 1,083 feet above sea level. The [[deciduous]] woodland which runs along it covers much of the steep slopes of the escarpment and in parts it is very well preserved. [[File:Eaton under Heywood 2012.JPG|300px|thumb|The Edge at [[Eaton under Heywood]]]] [[File:Jack Mytton Way - geograph.org.uk - 200927.jpg|thumb|[[Jack Mytton Way]], near Rushbury, Wenlock Edge, Shropshire]] It was featured on the 2005 TV programme ''[[Seven Natural Wonders]]'' as one of the wonders of the Midlands. Wenlock Edge contains many interesting features such as [[Flounders' Folly]], [[Wilderhope Manor]] and [[Shipton Hall]] and waymarked walks such as the [[Shropshire Way]] and [[bridleway]]s such as the [[Jack Mytton Way]]. It is a popular area for [[hillwalking]], cycling, [[mountain biking]] and [[horseback rider|horseriding]] and is also frequented by tourists and sightseers. [[Robert Hart (horticulturist)|Robert Hart]] created a model [[forest gardening|forest garden]] from a small orchard on his farm called Highwood Hill in Wenlock Edge.{{cite book|title=Forest Gardening|author=Robert Hart|year=1996|page=45|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=N01940btQAQC&q=forest%20gardening%20robert%20hart%20simple%20living&pg=PA45|isbn=9781603580502}} ==Geology== [[File:Llandovery and Wenlock Fossils Pocock Whitehead 1948 Figure 27 (Xylodes articulatus).jpg|thumb|left|150px|A fossil coral from the Wenlock Limestone{{cite book |last1=Pocock |first1=Roy Woodhouse |last2=Whitehouse |first2=T.H. |title=British Regional Geology: The Welsh Borderland 2nd Edition |date=1948 |publisher=His Majesty's Stationery Office (HMSO) |location=London |page=53 |url=https://archive.org/details/WelshBorderland2ndEdnBritishRegionalGeologyImages}}]] The "world famous Wenlock Limestone outcrops" are amongst "Britain’s most important geological sites". The limestone quarries in the North "demonstrate the best examples of [[reef]] development during the [[Silurian]] Period in Britain." Many species of [[brachiopods]], [[trilobite]]s and [[ostracod]] (microscopic crustaceans) were first found at Wenlock and most of the known [[Wenlock Series#Silurian fauna|Wenlock group Silurian fauna]] comes from here. [[Richard Corfield (scientist)|Richard Corfield]] also gave Wenlock Edge as an example of the most spectacular reef building the world has ever known.{{cite web|last=In Our Time|title=The Permian-Triassic Boundary|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b007r285|publisher=BBC|date=28 June 2007|access-date=30 June 2013}}
The reef was formed in shallow subtropical seas about 425 million years ago when the area was south of the equator at about the same latitude as the [[Seychelles]] is today.{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/shropshire/content/articles/2005/03/21/geological_tour_wenlock_edge.shtml|publisher=BBC Shropshire|title=Nature Features|date=October 2008|access-date=30 June 2013}} A walk by a BBC journalist in 2008 found abundant fossilised [[crinoids]] (sea lilies) and brachiopods. The [[Wenlock (Silurian)|Wenlock]] Epoch of the [[Silurian]] Period is named for the rocks of Wenlock Edge. == Legends== '''Ippikin''' Local legend tells of a local robber and bandit named Ippikin, who buried his ill-gotten gains in the vicinity of the edge. Tales tell that should anyone stand on the escarpment and say "Ippikin, Ippikin, keep away with your long chin" that they will be pushed over the edge by the ghost of the erstwhile villain.{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/shropshire/content/articles/2005/08/24/weird_ippikin_legend_feature.shtml|publisher=BBC Shropshire|title=Legends: Ippikin, the robber knight of Wenlock Edge|date=April 2008|access-date=30 June 2013}} '''Major's Leap''' In the [[English Civil War]] a Major Thomas Smallman of nearby [[Wilderhope Manor]] was a Royalist officer who was forced to flee from [[Oliver Cromwell|Cromwell's]] approaching troops after escaping from his manor. As he was carrying important dispatches, he was cornered on the Wenlock Edge. Rather than surrender, he galloped his horse off the edge falling some 200 feet. His horse was killed but the Major was saved by falling into an apple tree. He made his way on foot to [[Shrewsbury]] where he delivered the despatches. The area where he made the jump is known as Major's Leap and is said to be haunted by the Major and his horse. ==Transport== ===Rail=== Served by [[Transport for Wales Rail|Transport for Wales]] on the [[Welsh Marches Line]] and [[Heart of Wales Line]] at [[Church Stretton railway station|Church Stretton]] and [[Craven Arms railway station|Craven Arms]]. ===Bus=== 2012 saw the introduction of a Shropshire Hills Shuttle service that operates at weekends and on [[bank holiday]]s during the spring and summer. The route, called the "Wenlock Wanderer", connects the towns of [[Much Wenlock]] and [[Church Stretton]], and operates mostly along the B4371 which runs atop the Wenlock Edge. It also calls at [[Ticklerton]], [[Acton Scott]] and [[Marshbrook]] to the south of Church Stretton.[http://www.shropshirehillsaonb.co.uk/things-to-do/shuttles Shropshire Hills AONB] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110703011047/http://www.shropshirehillsaonb.co.uk/things-to-do/shuttles/ |date=3 July 2011 }} Shuttle bus service The Shrewsbury road down Wenlock Hill is one of the steepest main roads in the United Kingdom, with a gradient of 1 in 6.Harold Donaldson Eberlein – Little Known England – 2007 Page 12 "To the right the Shrewsbury road beckons us down Wenlock Hill, one of the hilliest main roads in the kingdom, with a gradient of 1 in 6 at steepest, unfolding a really fine view as you drop down into the vale with the Wrekin heaving up his broad ..." ==Cultural references== It is the setting for [[A. E. Housman]]'s poem "On Wenlock Edge the Wood's in Trouble", poem XXXI in his 1896 collection ''[[A Shropshire Lad]]''. In 1909, [[Ralph Vaughan Williams]] composed a [[song cycle]] called ''[[On Wenlock Edge (song cycle)|On Wenlock Edge]]'', which comprises settings of that and five other Housman poems. It is also the subject of several works by the famous artist [[L. S. Lowry]], with his piece ''A Bit of Wenlock Edge'', which is a fine pencil drawing of the escarpment, detailing the woodland.{{Citation needed|date=March 2018}} Housman's poem, in turn, is at the centre of a discussion in [[Alice Munro]]'s short story "Wenlock Edge". In his alternate history novel ''[[SS-GB]]'', set in a German-occupied Great Britain during [[World War II]], [[Len Deighton]] places a [[Gestapo]] concentration camp in Wenlock Edge.{{cite web |last=Glazzard |first=Andrew |date=12 February 2017 |title=Why thriller writers love to imagine Britain being invaded by Nazis |url=https://www.newstatesman.com/culture/2017/02/why-thriller-writers-love-imagine-britain-being-invaded-nazis |website=[[The New Statesman]] |access-date=2 August 2024}}{{cite book |author=Len Deighton |author-link=Len Deighton |date=1978 |title=[[SS-GB]] |edition=2023 |publisher=Penguin Books |page=275 |isbn=9780241639238}} ==References== {{reflist}} ==External links== * [http://www.amherst.edu/~rjyanco/literature/alfrededwardhousman/poems/ashropshirelad/onwenlockedgethewoodsintrouble.html On Wenlock Edge the Wood's in Trouble text] * [http://www3.shropshire-cc.gov.uk/walk01.htm Wenlock Edge – A Literary Walk] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20041205081303/http://www3.shropshire-cc.gov.uk/walk01.htm |date=5 December 2004 }} * [https://www.bbc.co.uk/england/sevenwonders/midlands/wenlock-edge/index.shtml BBC] * [https://wenlockedgenationaltrust.blogspot.com/ The National Trust's Blog for Wenlock Edge] {{Coord|52|33|1|N|2|39|17|W|type:mountain_region:GB-SHR|display=title}} [[Category:Escarpments of England]] [[Category:Geology of Shropshire]] [[Category:Hills of Shropshire]] [[Category:Sites of Special Scientific Interest in Shropshire]]

1374861.title: Brean Down
1374861.extract:
Brean Down is a promontory off the coast of Somerset, England, standing 318 feet (97 m) high and extending 1+1⁄2 miles (2.5 kilometres) into the Bristol Channel at the eastern end of Bridgwater Bay between Weston-super-Mare and Burnham-on-Sea.
Made of Carboniferous Limestone, it is a continuation of the Mendip Hills. Two further continuations are the small islands of Steep Holm and Flat Holm. The cliffs on the northern and southern flanks of Brean Down have large quantities of fossils laid down in the marine deposits about 320–350 million years ago. The site has been occupied by humans since the late Bronze Age and includes the remains of a Romano-Celtic Temple. At the seaward end is Brean Down Fort which was built in 1865 and then re-armed in the Second World War.
Brean Down is now owned by the National Trust, and is rich in wildlife, history and archaeology. It is a Site of Special Scientific Interest due to both the geology and presence of nationally rare plants including the white rock-rose. It has also been scheduled as an ancient monument.

3547066.title: Bath Assembly Rooms
3547066.extract:
The Bath Assembly Rooms, designed by John Wood, the Younger in 1769, are a set of assembly rooms located in the heart of the World Heritage City of Bath in England which are now open to the public as a visitor attraction. They are designated as a Grade I listed building.
During the Georgian era Bath became fashionable, and the architects John Wood, the Elder, and his son laid out new areas of housing for residents and visitors. Assembly rooms had been built early in the 18th century, but a new venue for balls, concerts and gambling was envisaged in the area between Queen Square, The Circus and the Royal Crescent. Robert Adam submitted a proposal that was rejected as too expensive. John Wood, the Younger raised funding through a tontine, and construction started in 1769. The new or upper assembly rooms opened with a grand ball in 1771 and became the hub of fashionable society, being frequented by Jane Austen and Charles Dickens, along with the nobility of the time.
The building, made of Bath stone, is arranged in a U shape. There are four main function rooms in the complex: the 100-foot-long (30 m) ballroom—the largest Georgian interior in Bath; the tea room; the card room; and the octagon. The rooms have Whitefriars crystal chandeliers and are decorated with fine art.
In the 20th century, they were used as a cinema, and in 1931, were taken over by the Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings and restored. They were bombed and burnt out during the Second World War, with restoration undertaken by Sir Albert Richardson before reopening in 1963. They are now owned and operated by the National Trust and were operated by Bath and North East Somerset Council for public functions until March 2023. The basement of the building provided a home to the Fashion Museum but this closed in October 2022 after a break clause in the lease was enacted. The exhibits have been placed into storage as the Museum seeks funding for a permanent new home within the city.

Assembly rooms had been built early in the 18th century, but a new venue for [[Ball (dance)|balls]], concerts and gambling was envisaged in the area between [[Queen Square (Bath)|Queen Square]], [[The Circus, Bath|The Circus]] and the [[Royal Crescent]]. [[Robert Adam]] submitted a proposal that was rejected as too expensive. John Wood, the Younger raised funding through a [[tontine]], and construction started in 1769. The new or upper assembly rooms opened with a grand ball in 1771 and became the hub of fashionable society, being frequented by [[Jane Austen]] and [[Charles Dickens]], along with the nobility of the time.

The building, made of [[Bath stone]], is arranged in a U shape. There are four main function rooms in the complex: the {{convert|100|ft|m|adj=mid|-long}} ballroom—the largest [[Georgian architecture|Georgian]] interior in Bath; the [[Tea house|tea room]]; the card room; and the octagon. The rooms have [[James Powell and Sons|Whitefriars crystal]] [[chandelier]]s and are decorated with fine art.

In the 20th century, they were used as a cinema, and in 1931, were taken over by the [[Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings]] and restored. They were bombed and burnt out during the [[Second World War]], with restoration undertaken by Sir [[Albert Richardson (architect)|Albert Richardson]] before reopening in 1963. They are now owned and operated by the [[National Trust]] and were operated by [[Bath and North East Somerset Council]] for public functions until March 2023. The basement of the building provided a home to the [[Fashion Museum, Bath|Fashion Museum]] but this closed in October 2022 after a break clause in the lease was enacted. The exhibits have been placed into storage as the Museum seeks funding for a permanent new home within the city.

==History==
Several areas of Bath had undergone development during the [[House of Stuart|Stuart]] period; development increased during [[Georgian era|Georgian]] times, however, in response to the increasing number of visitors to the spa and resort town who required accommodation.<!--
--><ref>{{cite book |title=The English Spa, 1560–1815: A Social History |last=Hembury |first=Phylis May |year=1990 |publisher=Fairleigh Dickinson Univ. Press |isbn=978-0-8386-3391-5}}<!--END--></ref> The architects [[John Wood, the Elder]] and his son [[John Wood, the Younger]] laid out the new quarters in streets and squares, the identical façades of which gave an impression of palatial scale and classical decorum.<!--
--><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bathmuseum.co.uk/biography.htm |title=John Wood and the Creation of Georgian Bath |access-date=8 December 2007 |work=Building of Bath Museum | archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20071113094712/http://www.bathmuseum.co.uk/biography.htm | archive-date=13 November 2007 |url-status=dead |df=dmy }}<!--END--></ref> Much of the creamy honey-coloured [[Bath stone]] used for construction throughout the city was obtained from the [[limestone]] [[Combe Down and Bathampton Down Mines]] owned by [[Ralph Allen]] (1694–1764).<!--
--><ref name="rabiog">{{cite web |url=http://www.bathpostalmuseum.co.uk/ralph-allen.html |title=Ralph Allen Biography |access-date=5 June 2012 |work=Bath Postal Museum |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004234025/http://www.bathpostalmuseum.co.uk/ralph-allen.html |archive-date=4 October 2013 |url-status=dead |df=dmy-all }}<!--END--></ref>

The development at this time largely consisted of new residential areas located away from the old city centre. The elder John Wood designed [[Queen Square (Bath)|Queen Square]], the [[Circus (Bath)|Circus]], and [[Gay Street, Bath|Gay Street]] in 1735, which would be completed by the younger John Wood.<!--
--><ref>{{cite book |title=The myth maker: John Wood 1704–1754 |last=Elliot |first=Kirsten |year=2004 |publisher=Akeman Press |isbn=978-0-9546138-2-2 |pages=57–68 }}<!--
END--></ref> Queen Square was the first speculative development by the elder John Wood, who lived in one of the houses.<!--
--><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ukattraction.com/west-country/queens-square.htm |title=Queen Square |access-date=10 January 2008 |work=UK attractions |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080419022417/http://www.ukattraction.com/west-country/queens-square.htm |archive-date = 19 April 2008|url-status=dead}}</ref><!--
--><ref>{{cite web |author=Historic England |author-link=Historic England |url=http://www.imagesofengland.org.uk/Details/Default.aspx?id=443387 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121018003651/http://www.imagesofengland.org.uk/Details/Default.aspx?id=443387 |url-status=dead |archive-date=2012-10-18 |title=Queen Square (north side) (443387) |work=[[Images of England]] }}<!--END--></ref> The [[Circus, Bath|Circus]] consists of three long, curved terraces that form a circular theatre intended for civic functions and games and inspired by the [[Colosseum]] in Rome.<!--
--><ref name="gadd">{{cite book |title=Georgian Summer |last=Gadd |first=David |year=1987 |publisher=Countryside Books }}<!--END--></ref> Finally, the elder Wood also designed and developed [[Gay Street, Bath|Gay Street]] which links the two; the buildings on Gay Street are now largely Grade I [[listed building]]s.

The most spectacular of Bath's terraces is the [[Royal Crescent]], designed by the younger John Wood, and built between 1767 and 1774.<!--
--><ref>{{cite web |author=Historic England |author-link=Historic England |url=http://www.imagesofengland.org.uk/Details/Default.aspx?id=447275 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071219035854/http://www.imagesofengland.org.uk/details/default.aspx?id=447275 |url-status=dead |archive-date=2007-12-19 |title=Royal Crescent (447275) |work=[[Images of England]] }}</ref>

The heart of the Georgian city was Wood's [[Grand Pump Room, Bath|Pump Room]], which, together with its associated Lower Assembly Rooms, was designed by [[Thomas Baldwin (architect)|Thomas Baldwin]], a local builder responsible for many other buildings in the city, including the terraces in Argyle Street<ref name="colvin">{{cite book |title=A Biographical Dictionary of British Architects, 1600–1840 |last=Colvin |first=Howard |author-link=Howard Colvin |isbn=0-300-07207-4 |year=1997 |publisher=Yale University Press |location=New Haven}}</ref> and the [[Guildhall, Bath|Guildhall]],<ref>{{cite web |author=Historic England |author-link=Historic England |url=http://www.imagesofengland.org.uk/Details/Default.aspx?id=442118 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120531182450/http://www.imagesofengland.org.uk/Details/Default.aspx?id=442118 |url-status=dead |archive-date=2012-05-31 |title=Guildhall (442118) |work=[[Images of England]]}}</ref> The Lower Assembly Rooms consisted of two buildings. The first built in 1708 for Thomas Harrison overlooking [[Parade Gardens]] between [[North Parade, Bath|North Parade]] and [[Bath Abbey]]. A large ballroom was added in 1720, with further enlargement in 1749 and 1810 when it became known as The Kingston Assembly Rooms. In 1728, another building, known as Lindsey's Assembly Rooms, was constructed, lasting until demolition around 1820 for the building of York Street. Harrison's Lower Assembly Rooms were devastated by a fire in December 1820 <ref>Taunton Courier 27 December 1820</ref> and rebuilt, lasting until demolition in 1933 for road improvements on the site now known as "Bog Island".<ref>{{cite web|last=Spence |first=Cathryn |title=The Lower Assembly Rooms, Bath |url=http://www.cathrynspence.com/?page_id=169 |publisher=Cathryn Spence |access-date=15 December 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131215141045/http://www.cathrynspence.com/?page_id=169 |archive-date=15 December 2013 |df=dmy}}</ref>

[[File:Fancy Dress Ball at the Bath Assembly Rooms by Thomas Rowlandson.jpg|thumb|left|Fancy Dress Ball at the Bath Assembly Rooms by [[Thomas Rowlandson]]]]
In around 1770, the [[neoclassicism|neoclassical]] architect [[Robert Adam]] designed [[Pulteney Bridge]], a three-arched bridge spanning the River Avon. He used as his prototype an original, but unused, design by [[Andrea Palladio]] for the [[Rialto Bridge]] in Venice.<ref name="pultney">{{cite journal |last=Manco |first=Jean |year=1995 |title=Pulteney Bridge |journal=[[Architectural History (journal)|Architectural History]]|volume=38 |pages=129–145 |doi=10.2307/1568625 |publisher=SAHGB Publications Limited |jstor=1568625 }}</ref> Adam also submitted plans for the new Assembly Rooms but these were rejected as too costly.<ref name=forsyth>{{cite book|last=Forsyth|first=Michael|title=Pevsner Architectural Guides: Bath|year=2003|publisher=Yale University Press|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HXrQN-GkmdYC&pg=PA88|isbn=978-0-300-10177-5|pages=88–91}}</ref> John Wood, the Younger raised funding for the construction of the Assembly Rooms by the use of a [[Tontine]], an investment plan that is named after the [[Naples|Neapolitan]] banker [[Lorenzo de Tonti]], who is credited with inventing it in [[France]] in 1653. It combines features of a group [[Life annuity|annuity]] and a [[lottery]]. Each subscriber pays an agreed sum into the fund, and thereafter receives an annuity. As members die, their shares devolve to the other participants, and so the value of each annuity increases. On the death of the last member, the scheme is wound up. Construction started in 1769 and was completed in 1771, when a grand opening was held.<ref name=knowles>{{cite web|last=Knowles |first=Rachel |title=The Upper Assembly Rooms, Bath |url=http://www.regencyhistory.net/2012/03/upper-assembly-rooms-bath.html |publisher=Regency History |access-date=14 December 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140317083847/http://www.regencyhistory.net/2012/03/upper-assembly-rooms-bath.html |archive-date=17 March 2014}}</ref>

The Assembly Rooms formed the hub of fashionable Georgian society in the city, the venue being described as "the most noble and elegant of any in the kingdom".<ref>{{cite web|title=Bath Assembly Rooms|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/bath-assembly-rooms/|publisher=National Trust|access-date=14 December 2013}}</ref> They were originally known as the Upper Rooms as there was also a lower assembly room in the city, which closed soon after the Upper Rooms opened. They served the newly built fashionable area which included the Circus, Queen Square and the Royal Crescent.<ref>{{cite web|title=Objects from the Collection|url=http://museumofbatharchitecture.org.uk/explore/objects-from-the-collection/|publisher=Museum of Bath Architecture|access-date=12 February 2017|archive-date=9 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160809075404/http://museumofbatharchitecture.org.uk/explore/objects-from-the-collection/|url-status=dead}}</ref>
[[File:Entrance to the Octagon.jpg|thumb|Entrance into the Octagon Room]]
People would gather in the rooms in the evening for balls and other public functions, or simply to play cards.<ref>{{cite book|last=Greeves|first=Lydia|title=Houses of the National Trust: Outstanding Buildings of Britain|year=2008|publisher=National Trust Books|isbn=978-1-905400-66-9|page=41|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LuD3gfEDiSYC&pg=PA42}}</ref> Mothers and chaperones bringing their daughters to Bath for the social season, hoping to marry them off to a suitable husband, would take their charge to such events where, very quickly, one might meet all the eligible men currently in the City. At one concert in 1779, attended by around 800 ladies and gentlemen, 60 members of the nobility were present.<ref>{{cite book|last1=McVeigh|first1=Simon|last2=Wollenberg |first2=Susan|title=Concert Life in Eighteenth-century Britain|year=2004|publisher=Ashgate Publishing|isbn=978-0-7546-3868-1|page=31 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jikJsI3jmvIC&pg=PA30}}</ref> During the season, which ran from October to June, at least two balls a week were held, in addition to a range of concerts and other events.<ref name=knowles/> Scenes such as this feature in the novels of [[Jane Austen]], who lived in Bath with her parents and sister from 1801 to 1805. Her two novels set in Bath, ''[[Northanger Abbey]]'' and ''[[Persuasion (novel)|Persuasion]]'', were published in 1818 and both mention the Assembly Rooms:
[[File:Pickwick Papers, la salle de jeux à Bath29.jpeg|thumb|left|1837 Steel engraving, probably by [[Hablot Knight Browne]], "The Card-room at Bath" used in ''[[The Pickwick Papers]]'']]
{{blockquote|text=Mrs Allen was so long in dressing, that they did not enter the ball-room till late. The season was full, the room crowded, and the two ladies squeezed in as well as they could. As for Mr Allen, he repaired directly to the card-room, and left them to enjoy a mob by themselves.|sign=[[Jane Austen]]|source=[[Northanger Abbey]]<ref>{{cite web|title=Assembly Rooms – Famous visitors|url=http://www.museumofcostume.co.uk/assembly_rooms/famous_visitors.aspx|publisher=Fashion Museum|access-date=14 December 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131216071500/http://museumofcostume.co.uk/assembly_rooms/famous_visitors.aspx|archive-date=16 December 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref>}}

{{blockquote|text=Sir Walter, his two daughters, and Mrs Clay, were the earliest of all their party at the rooms in the evening; and as Lady Dalrymple must be waited for, they took their station by one of the fires in the Octagon Room.|sign=[[Jane Austen]]|source=[[Persuasion (novel)|Persuasion]] (Chapter 20)<ref>{{cite web|title=Persuasion (Chapter 20)|url=http://www.publicbookshelf.com/romance/persuasion/door-opened-1|publisher=Public Bookshelf|access-date=14 December 2013}}</ref>}}

[[Charles Dickens]] also visited Bath on several occasions. He gave public readings in the Assembly Rooms and mentions them in ''[[The Pickwick Papers]]'' (published in 1837):
{{blockquote|text=In the ball-room, the long card-room, the octagonal card-room, the staircases, and the passages, the hum of many voices, and the sound of many feet, were perfectly bewildering. Dresses rustled, feathers waved, lights shone, and jewels sparkled. There was the music—not of the quadrille band, for it had not yet commenced; but the music of soft tiny footsteps, with now and then a clear merry laugh—low and gentle, but very pleasant to hear in a female voice, whether in Bath or elsewhere.|sign=[[Charles Dickens]]|source=[[The Pickwick Papers]]<ref>{{cite web|title=Chapter XXXV|url=http://www.victorianlondon.org/etexts/dickens/pickwick-0035.shtml|work=The Pickwick Papers, by Charles Dickens (1836–37)|publisher=Victorian Web|access-date=14 December 2013}}</ref>}}

[[George Bridgetower]], an [[African minority in Poland|Afro-Polish]]-born [[virtuoso]] [[violin]]ist, made his debut at the Assembly Rooms in 1789.<ref name=pastscape /> Another young violinist, [[Thomas Linley the younger]], played a series of concerts between 1771 and 1776. Many of the concerts during the late 18th and early 19th centuries were organised by [[Venanzio Rauzzini]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Bradley|first=Ian|title=Water Music: Making Music in the Spas of Europe and North America|year=2010|publisher=OUP|isbn=978-0-19-532734-2|pages=41–42|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WuEvbA2HnfIC&q=Bath+Assembly+Rooms+Concert&pg=PA41}}</ref>

In the 20th century, several changes took place, with the Ballroom becoming a cinema, until the [[Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings]] became the owners in 1931.<ref name=forsyth /><ref name=pastscape>{{PastScape|mname=Bath Assembly Rooms |mnumber=203830 |access-date=14 December 2013}}</ref> The building was restored by [[A Mowbray Green]] in 1938,<ref name=nhle /> with [[Oliver Messel]] as the interior designer.<ref name=forsyth /> During the [[Bath Blitz]] of 25/26 April 1942, one of the retaliatory raids on England by the [[Baedeker Blitz]] following the [[Bombing of Lübeck in World War II|RAF's raid]] on [[Lübeck]], the Assembly Rooms were bombed and burnt out inside. After the cessation of hostilities in Europe, they were restored by Sir [[Albert Richardson (architect)|Albert Richardson]], with work being completed in 1963. The ballroom ceiling had to be repaired after it collapsed in 1989.<ref name=nhle />

==Architecture==
[[File:Bath Assembly Rooms - Tea Room.jpg|thumb|Three chandeliers adorning the Tea Room]]
The [[limestone]] building has a slate [[Hip roof|hipped roof]]. It is rectangular with a projecting [[Doric order|doric]] [[portico]] entrance and an extension to the rear.<ref name=nhle/> The interior is laid out in a U shape, with the larger Ball Room and Tea Room along either side with the octagonal Card Room at the end.<ref name=knowles/> The rooms have [[James Powell and Sons|Whitefriars crystal]] [[chandelier]]s and are decorated with pictures by [[Thomas Gainsborough]], [[Allan Ramsay (artist)]], [[Edwin Long]] and [[William Hoare]].<ref name="banes">{{cite web |title=The Assembly Rooms Bath |url=http://www.bathvenues.co.uk/assembly_rooms.aspx |access-date=14 December 2013 |work=Bath's Historic Buildings |publisher=Bath and North East Somerset Council |archive-date=3 January 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150103173805/http://www.bathvenues.co.uk/assembly_rooms.aspx |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=William Hoare|url=https://artuk.org/discover/artworks/self-portrait-40049|work=Your paintings|publisher=BBC|access-date=14 December 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Edwin Long|url=https://artuk.org/discover/artworks/thomas-barrett-18151868-jp-md-40139|work=Your paintings|publisher=BBC|access-date=14 December 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Allan Ramsey|url=https://artuk.org/discover/artworks/george-iii-17381820-40228|work=Your paintings|publisher=BBC|access-date=14 December 2013}}</ref>

The Ballroom has five chandeliers and capacity for up to 500 people.<ref>{{cite web|title=Ball Room|url=http://www.bathvenues.co.uk/assembly_rooms/ball_room.aspx|work=Bath's Historic Buildings|publisher=Bath and North East Somerset council|access-date=14 December 2013|archive-date=23 February 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140223161150/http://www.bathvenues.co.uk/assembly_rooms/ball_room.aspx|url-status=dead}}</ref> It is over {{convert|100|ft}} long and nearly {{convert|45|ft}} wide.<ref name=knowles/> The ceiling is {{convert|42|ft}} high.<ref name=nhle/> The Tea Room holds up to 250 people. It was the location for a banquet attended by [[Charles, Prince of Wales]] for the BBC television series the [[Great British Menu]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Tea Room|url=http://www.bathvenues.co.uk/assembly_rooms/tea_room.aspx|work=Bath's Historic Buildings|publisher=Bath and North east Somerset council|access-date=14 December 2013|archive-date=15 December 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131215141223/http://www.bathvenues.co.uk/assembly_rooms/tea_room.aspx|url-status=dead}}</ref> It is {{convert|60|ft}} long and {{convert|42|ft}} wide.<ref name=nhle/> The Octagon is named for the shape of the room and has four fireplaces.<ref>{{cite web|title=Octagon|url=http://www.bathvenues.co.uk/assembly_rooms/octagon.aspx|work=Bath's Historic Buildings|publisher=Bath and North east Somerset council|access-date=14 December 2013}}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> It is {{convert|42|ft}} across.<ref name=nhle/> It originally held an organ in the musicians gallery.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Upper Rooms|url=http://www.janeausten.co.uk/the-upper-rooms/|publisher=Jane Austen.co.uk|access-date=14 December 2013|archive-date=15 December 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131215141550/http://www.janeausten.co.uk/the-upper-rooms/|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 1777, the Card Room was added.{{Cn|date=December 2023}}

[[Philip Thicknesse]] in his 1778 'New Bath Guide' admired the architecture of the New or Upper Rooms but thought that 'in spite of all these Advantages, we much doubt, whether it be true that the Upper Rooms shew Female Beauty so advantageously ''as the Lower....'' We have examined too, with a Degree of  particular Attention, some of the most Admired Beauties of the last and present season, at both the Rooms, and, as far as we could determine, they were either best pleased, or most beautiful, under the ''lower'' than the ''upper lights'.''<ref>Thicknesse, Philip (1778) The New Prose Bath Guide, for the Year 1778, 2nd, ed. London & Bath, p. 37.</ref>

==Current use==
[[File:Octagon Room.jpg|thumb|The Octagon Room, with a central chandelier]]
Today, the rooms are owned and operated by the [[National Trust]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bath Assembly Rooms project {{!}} Bath |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/bath-bristol/bath-assembly-rooms/future-plans-for-bath-assembly-rooms |access-date=2023-05-21 |website=National Trust |language=en}}</ref> They are used currently used as a venue for partnership exhibitions and concerts, including ones that are part of the [[Bath International Music Festival]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Bath International Music Festival 2016|url=http://bathfestivals.org.uk/music/bath-international-music-festival-2016-eleven-events-on-early-release-full-programme-announcement/|publisher=Bath International Music Festival|access-date=12 February 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160402100857/http://bathfestivals.org.uk/music/bath-international-music-festival-2016-eleven-events-on-early-release-full-programme-announcement/|archive-date=2 April 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Evans|first=Rian|title=Bath Mozartfest|url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2008/nov/11/classicalmusicandopera|access-date=14 December 2013|newspaper=Guardian|date=11 November 2008}}</ref>

The basement of the building provided a home to the [[Fashion Museum, Bath|Fashion Museum]], which was known before 2007 as the Museum of Costume, until its closure in October 2022.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-06-14 |title=Plans for the future of the Fashion Museum |url=https://www.fashionmuseum.co.uk/news/plans-future-fashion-museum |access-date=2023-05-21 |website=Fashion Museum Bath |language=en}}</ref> The collection was started by [[Doris Langley Moore]], who gave her collection to the city of Bath in 1963. It focuses on [[fashion]]able dress for men, women and children from the late 16th century to the present day and has more than 30,000 objects. The earliest pieces are [[embroidery|embroidered]] [[shirt]]s and [[glove]]s from about 1600.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.culture24.org.uk/sw000051 |title=Fashion museum, Bath |access-date=14 December 2013 |work=24 hour museum |publisher=Culture 24}}</ref>

The grandeur of the building make it a popular location for feature films and television series set in the Georgian period. The BBC have used it as a location for the filming of an adaptation of [[Northanger Abbey (1986 film)|''Northanger Abbey'' in 1986]] and in [[Persuasion (1995 film)|1995 ''Persuasion'']].<ref>{{cite web|title=Bath as a film location|url=https://www.fashionmuseum.co.uk/filming-and-photography|publisher=Museum of Costume|access-date=15 July 2017|archive-date=8 April 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160408165427/http://www.fashionmuseum.co.uk/filming-and-photography|url-status=dead}}</ref> The Assembly Rooms were also used as a location for several scenes in [[Bridgerton]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-03-09 |title=Bath's Starring Role in Bridgerton |url=https://visitbath.co.uk/blog/read/2022/03/baths-starring-role-in-bridgerton-b86 |access-date=2023-05-21 |website=Visit Bath |language=en-GB}}</ref>

3846145.title: Barrington Court
3846145.extract:
Barrington Court is a Tudor manor house begun around 1538 and completed in the late 1550s, with a vernacular stable court (1675), situated in Barrington, near Ilminster, Somerset, England.
The house was owned by several families by 1745 after which it fell into disrepair and was used as a tenant farm. After repair by architect Alfred Hoare Powell (1865–1960), it was acquired by the National Trust in 1907, on the recommendation of the antiquarian Canon Hardwicke Rawnsley (1851–1920). 
It has been described as the first house acquired by the National Trust, although Alfriston Clergy House, a more modest property, was acquired earlier.
In the 1920s the house was renovated after Colonel Lyle and his wife 'Ronnie' agreed to take on a ninety-nine year repairing lease from the Trust, and work began in 1921. The stable block turned into a residence and several outbuildings, gardens and gateways were constructed.
The house was originally surrounded by a medieval deer park and in the 17th century a formal garden was constructed. This had largely disappeared until a new garden was laid out by garden designer Gertrude Jekyll (1843–1932) in an Arts and Crafts-style. It now contains walled kitchen gardens, fruit orchards and ornamental gardens.
