'''Barrington Court''' is a [[Tudor architecture|Tudor]] [[manor house]] begun around 1538 and completed in the late 1550s, with a vernacular stable court (1675), situated in [[Barrington, Somerset|Barrington]], near [[Ilminster]], [[Somerset]], England.

The house was owned by several families by 1745 after which it fell into disrepair and was used as a [[tenant farmer|tenant farm]]. After repair by architect [[Alfred Hoare Powell]] (1865–1960), it was acquired by the [[National Trust]] in 1907, on the recommendation of the antiquarian Canon [[Hardwicke Rawnsley]] (1851–1920).<ref name=sher/> 
It has been described as the first house acquired by the National Trust, although [[Alfriston Clergy House]], a more modest property, was acquired earlier.
In the 1920s the house was renovated after Colonel Lyle and his wife 'Ronnie' agreed to take on a ninety-nine year repairing lease from the Trust, and work began in 1921.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/barrington-court/features/craftsmanship-exemplified-|title = Craftsmanship exemplified}}</ref> The stable block turned into a residence and several outbuildings, gardens and gateways were constructed.

The house was originally surrounded by a [[medieval deer park]] and in the 17th century a formal garden was constructed. This had largely disappeared until a new garden was laid out by [[garden designer]] [[Gertrude Jekyll]] (1843–1932) in an [[Arts and Crafts]]-style. It now contains walled kitchen gardens, fruit orchards and ornamental gardens.

==History==
The estate had been occupied since the 11th century and by the 14th century included a substantial house to the north east of the present building, where traces of a moat can still be seen. In 1446 the owner, [[Giles Daubeney, 6th Baron Daubeney]], died at Barrington and left it to his son, another Giles Daubeney, [[Giles Daubeney, 1st Baron Daubeney]] who was a courtier, diplomat and military commander under [[Edward IV]] and [[Henry VII of England|Henry VII]].<ref name=dunning>{{Cite book |last=Dunning |first=Robert |year=1991 |title=Some Somerset Country Houses |publisher=Dovecote Press |location=Wimborne |isbn=978-0-946159-85-7 |pages=13–16}}</ref>

[[File:Barringtoncourt1.jpg|thumb|left|The south front]]
The manor was inherited in 1514 by [[Henry Daubeney, 1st Earl of Bridgewater|Henry Daubeney]], created [[Earl of Bridgewater]] for his services to [[Henry VIII]]. He spent much of his time in France and little time in Somerset.<ref name=dunning/> He may have begun the new house, but he went bankrupt. He married a Catherine Howard. <ref name=sher/> It is unlikely that much, if any, of the current building was his work.<ref name=dunning/> The house was forfeit to the crown and then had various owners including [[Henry Grey, 1st Duke of Suffolk]], who in 1552 sold it to William Clifton, a London merchant who had been assembling a Somerset estate.<ref>{{cite web |editor-first=R.W. |editor-last=Dunning |first1=A.P. |last1=Baggs |first2=R.J.E. |last2=Bush |year=1978 |url=http://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/som/vol4/pp113-121 |title=Parishes: Barrington |publisher=Institute of Historical Research |work=A History of the County of Somerset: Volume 4 |access-date=29 September 2015 }}</ref> Clifton or his son John Clifton are thought to be responsible for most of the building at Barrington, possibly modeled on earlier work at [[Kirby Hall]] or East Anglian manors close to their roots at [[Kentwell Hall]], [[Hengrave Hall]] or [[Channonz Hall]] at [[Tibenham, Norfolk|Tibenham]].<ref name=dunning/>

It passed down in the Clifton family including [[Gervase Clifton, 1st Baron Clifton|Gervase Clifton]], who in 1605 sold it to his brother-in-law Sir Thomas Phelips of [[Montacute House]]. The house was then mortgaged and, in 1625, sold to Colonel [[William Strode (of Barrington)|William Strode, Jr]].<ref name=dunning/> The house and estate were owned by the Strode family from 1625 until 1745 after which it was bought by several different owners but poorly maintained,<ref name=sher/> becoming known as Court Farm.<ref name=dunning/>

The interior of the house suffered from its demotion to a [[tenant farmer|tenant farm]] and from a fire in the early 19th century; after being almost derelict it was repaired under the supervision of [[Alfred Hoare Powell]]. Barrington Court was acquired by the [[National Trust]] in 1907 and was leased to Col. Abram Arthur Lyle of [[Tate & Lyle]] in the 1920s.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Greenwood |first=Charles |year=1977 |title=Famous houses of the West Country |publisher=Kingsmead Press |location=Bath |isbn=978-0-901571-87-8 |pages=1–3}}</ref> Abram Lyle and his wife, Elsie Ronalds Lyle (née. Crowdy and known as 'Ronnie') turned the house around and refurbished the court house and renovated Strode House (built by Colonel Strode's son, [[William Strode III (of Barrington)|William III]], in 1674) which was originally a stable and coach block. It was at this time that the Lyles contracted [[Gertrude Jekyll]] to design the three formal gardens on the property that are maintained by the head gardener.<ref name=sher/>

The house was one of the first large properties acquired by the National Trust; it was not anticipated just how expensive repairs and maintenance would be, and even thirty years later it was still used as an example of why the Trust should be wary of taking on other country houses.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Waterson |first=Merlin |year=1994 |title=The National Trust: The First Hundred Years |publisher=BBC Books |isbn=978-0-563-37066-6 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/nationaltrustfir00wate/page/50 50–52] |url=https://archive.org/details/nationaltrustfir00wate/page/50 }}</ref>

Barrington Court was occupied by a tenant, Stuart Interiors, that took the lease in 1986 from Andrew Lyle, grandson of Col. Lyle. The company sold reproduction furniture.<ref>{{cite web|title=An Invitation to Barrington Court |work=Stuart Interiors |url=http://www.stuartinteriors.ltd.uk/visit5.php |access-date=15 October 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071008144015/http://www.stuartinteriors.ltd.uk/visit5.php |archive-date=8 October 2007 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Stuart Interiors left Barrington Court in December 2008, and although the building has no furniture, it is open to visitors.<ref>{{cite web|title=Breathing life back into Barrington Court |url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-vh/w-visits/w-findaplace/w-barringtoncourt/w-barrington_court-rescue.htm |publisher=National Trust |access-date=6 October 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100810022028/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-vh/w-visits/w-findaplace/w-barringtoncourt/w-barrington_court-rescue.htm |archive-date=10 August 2010 }}</ref>

==Architecture==

Like many [[Elizabethan architecture|Elizabethan]] [[mansion]]s, Barrington is built in an 'E' shape with large projecting wings with square projections that contain staircases.<ref name=sher/> The house is not truly symmetrical as the hall has two [[window|lights]] and the buttery one. The south front has seven gables supported by octagonal buttresses<ref name=sher/> and decorated with twisted [[finial]]s with [[ogee]] scale-work caps and English [[Crocket]]s.<ref name=dunning/>

Its central entry porch leads into a screens passage with the [[hall]] on the left and, an innovation, a service passage leading to the kitchen wing that occupies the right wing.<ref name=cooper/> A [[long gallery]] stretches the entire length of the house on the upper floor.<ref name=dunning/>

===Strode House===
[[File:Strode House, Barrington Court - geograph.org.uk - 1311639.jpg|thumb|left|Strode House]]
The stables – built in 1674 by [[William Strode III (of Barrington)|William Strode III]] – were converted into a separate house around 1920, under plans drawn up by the architect J.E. Forbes, when the building was given a new west front.<ref name=sher>{{cite web |title=Barrington Court Park, Barrington |url=http://www.somersetheritage.org.uk/record/55164 |work=Somerset Historic Environment Record |publisher=Somerset County Council |access-date=17 March 2013}}</ref> The two-storey brick building has [[Hamstone]] dressings and a [[Hip roof|hipped]] tile roof. Immediately in front of the building is the "fountain court".<ref name=wing/>

===Outbuildings===

In the 1920s a "motorhouse" was constructed in a Tudor style to match the other buildings. It is a single-storey building with an attic. The front of the building is decorate with heraldic lions.<ref>{{NHLE |desc=Motorhouse |num=1264739 |access-date=18 March 2013}}</ref>

The two-storey agent's house, known as Beechams, was also built in the 1920s.<ref>{{NHLE |desc=Beechams |num=1236233 |access-date=18 March 2013}}</ref> There are also row of six thatched cottages in Tudor style, a farmhouse and a barn dating from the same period.<ref>{{NHLE |desc=Barrington Court Cottages |num=1236207 |access-date=18 March 2013}}</ref><ref>{{NHLE |desc=Barrington Court Farmhouse |num=1056937 |access-date=18 March 2013}}</ref><ref>{{NHLE |desc=Store and barn |num=1056936 |access-date=18 March 2013}}</ref>

===Gateways and walls===

[[File:Gateway to East of South Lawn of Barrington Court.jpg|thumb|View of Gateway to East of South Lawn of Barrington Court]]There are multiple gateways around the estate and entrances to the house. The gateway to the west of the forecourt was rebuilt in the 1920s with tall piers and moulded stepped caps, permitting a full view of the symmetrical facade of the house.<ref name=cooper>{{Cite book |last=Cooper |first=Nicholas |year=1999 |title=Houses of the Gentry, 1480–1680 |publisher=Yale University Press |isbn=978-0-300-07390-4 |pages=75–78}}</ref><ref>{{NHLE |desc=Gateway to west of forecourt |num=1056934 |access-date=18 March 2013}}</ref> The gateways to the east of the forecourt and to the east of the south lawn have [[wrought iron]] gates.<ref>{{NHLE |desc=Gateway to east of forecourt |num=1056933 |access-date=18 March 2013}}</ref><ref>{{NHLE |desc=Gateway to east of south lawn |num=1345922 |access-date=18 March 2013}}</ref> The wall around the forecourt is of the same vintage and has rectangular lily ponds at the base.<ref>{{NHLE |desc=Walls bounding main entrance to forecourt garden |num=1345921 |access-date=18 March 2013}}</ref>

==Gardens==
[[File:Barringtonct1.jpg|thumb|upright|Part of house and gardens at Barrington Court in late summer]]

In the 16th century the house was surrounded by a [[Medieval deer park|deer park]]. In the 1550s William Clifton took action, in the [[Star Chamber]] court, against local poachers who hunted deer in the park while he was away.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bond |first=James |year=1998 |title=Somerset parks and gardens: A landscape history |publisher=Somerset Books |location=Tiverton |isbn=978-0-86183-465-5 |pages=54, 57}}</ref>

The remains of the original gardens include a rectangular raised area or [[parterre]] {{convert|70|m}} by {{convert|50|m}} near a liner pond or canal which is {{convert|12|m}} by {{convert|110|m}}.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.somersetheritage.org.uk/record/31374 |title=Garden earthworks, E of Barrington Court |work=Somerset Historic Environment Record |publisher=Somerset County Council |access-date=18 March 2013}}</ref> There is also geophysical evidence of a further 17th-century formal garden.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.somersetheritage.org.uk/record/31389 |title=Seventeenth-century formal garden site, S of Barrington Court |work=Somerset Historic Environment Record |publisher=Somerset County Council |access-date=18 March 2013}}</ref>

Barrington Court is noted for its [[Arts and Crafts]]-style [[garden]]s for which [[garden design]]er Gertrude Jekyll provided planting plans.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Jekyll |first=Gertrude |year=1908 |title=Colour in the Flower Garden}}</ref> The gardens were laid out in 1917 by J. E. Forbes, of the partnership Forbes & Tate, for Lieut-Col. A. Arthur Lyle. There are a series of walled areas that include a [[white garden]], a [[rose]] and [[Iris (plant)|iris]] garden and a [[lily]] garden.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Plumptree |first=George |year=1985 |title=Collins Book of British Gardens |publisher=Collins |location=London |isbn=0-00-216641-0 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/collinsbookofbri00plum/page/267 267–269] |url=https://archive.org/details/collinsbookofbri00plum/page/267 }}</ref> The original plans are being used to restore the gardens; however, the planting scheme has been changed from that designed by Jekyll to that designed by Mrs Lyle in the 1960s.<ref name=bond138to139/>

The walls of the kitchen garden were built in the 1920s and include two gateways with [[Neoclassical architecture|neoclassical]] architraves.<ref name=walled/> The gravel paths are laid out in a square with a cross at the centre enhanced by a fountain surrounded by fruit trees, vegetable plots and soft fruits.<ref name=bond138to139>{{Cite book |last=Bond |first=James |year=1998 |title=Somerset parks and gardens: A landscape history |publisher=Somerset Books |location=Tiverton |isbn=978-0-86183-465-5 |pages=138–139}}</ref> There are carriage openings with wrought-iron gates.<ref name=walled>{{NHLE |desc=Walled garden and attached squash court |num=1345923 |access-date=18 March 2013}}</ref>

[[File:Bizarre Sundial outside Barrington Court - panoramio.jpg|thumb|left|Unusual multi-faced [[sundial]]]]

The kitchen garden provides produce for the property's restaurant located in the adjacent Strode House; this includes many types of fruit and vegetables. The local St Mary & St Peter's CE VC Primary School, which has bases at Barrington and Ilton, has a vegetable plot where the children plant, tend and cook the produce; the walls are also strewn with apple, pear and plum trees. Attached to the garden is a squash court.<ref name=walled/>

About {{convert|20|m}} south west of the house is an unusual multi-faced [[sundial]].<ref name=sher/> It was built of stone and bronze, on a stone column.<ref>{{cite web|title=Sundial|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/262261|publisher=National Trust|access-date=23 March 2014}}</ref> It is a [[dodecahedron]] surmounted by a heraldic lion. It was imported from California by Colonel Lyle in 1920.<ref>{{cite book|last=Byford|first=Enid|title=Somerset Curiosities|date=1987|publisher=Dovecote Press|isbn=0946159483|pages=[https://archive.org/details/somersetcuriosit0000byfo/page/41 41–42]|url=https://archive.org/details/somersetcuriosit0000byfo/page/41}}</ref>

The gardens are Grade II* listed on the [[National Register of Historic Parks and Gardens]].<ref>{{NHLE |desc=Barrington Court |num=1000505 |access-date=17 March 2013}}</ref>

==Popular culture==

Author Andrew Norman has argued that Barrington Court was the inspiration for 'Kellynch Hall' in [[Jane Austen]]'s ''[[Persuasion (novel)|Persuasion]]''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Norman |first1=Andrew |title=Jane Austen: Love is Like a Rose |date=2015 |publisher=Fonthill Media |isbn=1781554420}}</ref>

In 2014 it was the site of filming for the BBC's Tudor-era historical TV serial ''[[Wolf Hall (TV series)|Wolf Hall]]''.<ref name=bbc>{{cite news|last1=Frith-Salem|first1=Benjamin|title=Wolf Halls: take a look inside the properties where the new BBC series is filmed|url=http://www.historyextra.com/feature/tudors/wolf-halls-take-look-inside-properties-where-new-bbc-series-filmed|access-date=25 January 2015|publisher=BBC History Magazine|date=20 January 2015}}</ref> In May 2015 the house was the venue for the BBC programme ''[[Antiques Roadshow]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b05whdnw|title=BBC One – Antiques Roadshow, Series 37, Barrington Court 1}}</ref>

'''Sunnycroft''' is a [[Victorian era|Victorian]] [[suburb]]an villa, located in [[Wellington, Shropshire]], and owned by the [[National Trust]].<ref name=s>{{cite web|title=Sunnycroft|access-date =7 July 2025|url=https://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/place/sunnycroft|publisher= [[National Trust]]}}</ref>

== Location ==
The house is located in the [[market town]] of Wellington, Shropshire, England, close to the town centre, on the [[B5061 road|B5061]] Holyhead Road, originally the [[Shrewsbury]] to London road, and formerly part of [[Watling Street]] the [[Roman roads|Roman road]] from London to [[Wroxeter]].

==History==
Suburban villas were almost 'country estates in miniature' which attempted to emulate [[upper class]] [[mansion]]s on a [[middle class]] budget. Many have either been modernised, renovated or refurbished out of recognition over the last 60 years or so or have been demolished and replaced with later housing, converted into offices or residential care homes, or have been broken up into flats and smaller residences.

Sunnycroft was built in 1879 and extended in 1899.<ref>{{cite web|title=A brief history|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/shropshire-staffordshire/sunnycroft/the-house-at-sunnycroft|publisher= [[National Trust]]|access-date=7 July 2025}}</ref> It was built by brewer J. G. Wackrill and later owned by Mary Jane Slaney, a local wine and spirit merchant. From 1912 it was owned and occupied by the Lander family, until it was acquired by the National Trust in 1997. Many of the original interior fixtures and fittings remain in place, although electricity was installed by the Lander family. Many original features are still in place and the house therefore has a unique character and intimacy that is often lacking from larger properties but very evocative of its time and place.

The National Trust summarises Sunnycroft as a late 19th-century gentleman's villa, a typical creation of [[Victorian era]] [[suburbia]], with:
* a rare unaltered interior, with an elaborate [[sunroom|conservatory]]
* a mini country-estate, with [[pigsties]], [[stables]], [[kitchen garden]] and [[orchard]]s
* colourful borders and summertime flower displays
* a superb long avenue of [[Redwood tree|Redwood]] trees and [[lime tree]]s.

==Access==
{{asof|2025}} the National Trust opens the property to the public on a limited number of occasions and otherwise by appointment.<ref name=s />

13340690.title: Burrow Mump
13340690.extract:
Burrow Mump is a hill and historic site overlooking Southlake Moor in the village of Burrowbridge within the English county of Somerset. It is a scheduled monument, with a never completed church on top of the hill a Grade II listed building.
The hill stands at a strategic location overlooking the point where the River Tone and the old course of the River Cary join the River Parrett. Although there is some evidence of Roman visitation, the first fortification of the site was the construction of a Norman motte. It has been called King Alfred's Fort, however there is no proof of use by Alfred the Great. A medieval church was built on the hill in the 15th century. The current ruined church on top of the hill was built in 1793. The land and ruin were donated to the National Trust in 1946 as a war memorial.

'''Wilderhope Manor''' is a 16th-century [[manor house]] in the care of the [[National Trust]]. It is located on [[Wenlock Edge]] {{convert|7|mi|km}} south west of [[Much Wenlock]] in [[Shropshire]], [[England]].  The manor is a Grade I [[listed building]] and since 1937 has been used as a [[youth hostel]].

== History and amenities ==
[[File:Wilderhope Manor, Rushbury - geograph.org.uk - 69335.jpg|thumb|Wilderhope Manor from the rear]]
Wilderhope Manor is an [[Elizabethan architecture|Elizabethan]]-period [[manor house]], built of local [[limestone]]  and dating from 1585. The house was built for Francis Smallman and his initials can be seen on the ceilings.{{sfn|Currie|1998|p=57}}  The manor remained in the family until 1734 when the estate including the neighbouring Wilderhope farm was sold to [[Thomas Lutwyche]].{{sfn|Currie|1998|p=57}}  It is believed that the manor house was not used as a main residence after the sale in 1734 and by 1936 was in a poor state and unoccupied.{{sfn|Currie|1998|p=58}}  In 1936 the property was purchased by the [[William Adlington Cadbury|W. A. Cadbury Trust]] who donated it to the National Trust on condition that it was used as a youth hostel.{{sfn|The Youth Hosteller|May 1959|p=9}}  Opening as a youth hostel in 1937,{{sfn|The Youth Hosteller|May 1959|p=9}} it has remained in use by the [[Youth Hostels Association (England & Wales)|Youth Hostels Association]] since.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.yha.org.uk/hostel/wilderhope |title=YHA Wilderhope |date=2012 |access-date=20 October 2012 |publisher=YHA}}</ref> A £500,000 refurbishment was completed in 2012 and the youth hostel offers 72 beds including a bridal suite with a [[four-poster bed]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Northern Design Awards |url=https://entries.northerndesignawards.com/entry/2012/wilderhope-manor-0 |access-date=8 December 2019}}</ref>

Despite years of disuse many of the original features such as the oaken stairways, oak spiral stairs and ornate [[plasterwork|plaster ceilings]] survived.<ref name=NHLE/>  The adjoining stable block is itself a [[Grade II listed building]].<ref>{{NHLE |num=1383385 |desc=Wilderhope Manor Stables|accessdate=20 October 2012}}</ref>

The manor house is in limestone with dressings in [[gritstone]], [[quoin (architecture)|quoins]], [[hood mould]]s, [[coping (architecture)|copings]] and [[finial]]s on the front, and a stone-slate roof.  There are two storeys and attics, and an approximately H-shaped plan.  The entrance front has six [[bay (architecture)|bays]] and four unequal [[gable]]s, three of them over projecting bays.  In the left projecting gable is a porch, the windows are [[mullion]]ed and [[transom (architecture)|transomed]], and at the rear is a semicircular stair turret with a conical roof.{{sfnp|Newman|Pevsner|2006|p=702|ps=none}}{{sfnp|Historic England|1383384|ps=none}}

The stables, now used for other purposes, are in brick with a [[belt course|storey band]], and have tile roofs with [[parapet]]ed gables.  They have a single storey and lofts, and a U-shaped plan with a main range of three bays.  The windows are [[casement window|casements]] with segmental arches, and there are doorways and loft openings.{{sfnp|Newman|Pevsner|2006|p=702|ps=none}}{{sfnp|Historic England|1383385|ps=none}}

The surrounding [[manorialism|manor]] of Wilderhope is also managed by the National Trust and comprises wooded valleys, pasture, flower-rich meadows and ancient hedgerows dating back centuries along unchanged field boundaries. Evidence of [[medieval]] [[ridge and furrow]] ploughing can still be seen in fields below Wilderhope Coppice.<ref>{{cite web |title=Wenlock Edge info |url=http://wenlockedgenationaltrust.blogspot.co.uk/2010/08/wenlock-edge-info.html |date=30 August 2012 |publisher=National Trust |access-date=20 October 2012}}</ref>

== Major's Leap ==
The Manor's owner during  the [[English Civil War]] was Major Thomas Smallman. He was a [[Cavalier|Royalist]] who was forced to flee from [[Oliver Cromwell|Cromwell]]’s approaching troops. After managing to escape on horseback, Major Smallman took a do-or-die plunge down a steep slope at [[Wenlock Edge]]. His horse was killed but Smallman survived thanks to an apple tree breaking his fall. Since then the ghosts of Smallman and his horse are said to appear in an area now known as Major's Leap and have been said to have been seen at the manor.{{sfn|Nicolle|2003|p=102}}

'''Town Walls Tower''' (officially '''Wingfield's Tower''') is the last remaining [[medieval]] watchtower belonging to the former [[Defensive walls|town walls]] of [[Shrewsbury]], [[Shropshire]], [[England]]. The fortified structure, which was finished in the 14th century, was used to observe the land south of the town and across [[River Severn]]. It is under the care of the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]].

== History ==
Shrewsbury town walls were completed in stone in the 13th century replacing earlier ramparts. Work to fortify the settlement had started immediately after the [[Angles (tribe)|Angles]], under King [[Offa of Mercia]], took possession in 778 CE. A century later the [[Anglo-Saxon England|Anglo-Saxon]]s had strengthened the town earthworks with a wide ditch and rampart that was topped with a wooden stockade.<ref name="localhistories.org">{{cite web |url=http://www.localhistories.org/shrewsbury.html |last=Lambert |first=Tim |title=Saxon and Medieval Shrewsbury |work=A Short History of Shrewsbury, Shropshire, England |publisher=A World History Encyclopaedia |url-status=live |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120315203401/http://www.localhistories.org/shrewsbury.html |archivedate=15 March 2012 |df=dmy-all }}</ref> 
Most of the early defences were adjacent to the river because its size, depth and limited crossing points provided a substantial defence to direct attack.

In 1070 the Normans started [[Shrewsbury Castle]] at the north end of the settlement but did not alter the settlement's outer defences.<ref name="town">{{cite web|url=https://shrewsburylocalhistory.org.uk/street-names/town-walls|title=Town Walls|website=shrewsburylocalhistory.org.uk|accessdate=22 April 2024|archive-date=22 April 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240422222211/https://shrewsburylocalhistory.org.uk/street-names/town-walls|url-status=live}}</ref>

However, by early 13th century, [[List of Anglo-Welsh wars|military action]] was increasing between the Welsh and the English. In 1215 [[Llywelyn ap Iorwerth]] overran the Anglo-Saxon earthworks and ramparts, sacking and burning Shrewsbury. This prompted [[Henry III of England|Henry III]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Attingham Park Estate: Town Walls Tower |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/shropshire-staffordshire/www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/shropshire-staffordshire/attingham-park-estate-town-walls-tower |access-date=2022-12-31 |website=National Trust |language=en}}</ref> in 1218 to command the town's [[aldermen]] to improve its defences. Through [[murage]], the town walls were extended, upgraded and repaired, watch towers were added and new gates with towers were also installed (the North Gate was given a drawbridge). The walls, which were {{convert|1.8|m|abbr=on}} thick, were constructed from sandstone; a plinth was built into the base of its outer face and there was an external ditch. By 1242, further work had added an outer earthen bank that was {{convert|2|m|abbr=on}} high and {{convert|9|m|abbr=on}} wide.<ref name="town"/>

During this period the Town Walls Tower would have been used by the town garrison to watch the surrounding area for Welsh incursions and raids. However, after the [[Conquest of Wales by Edward I of England|pacification of the Welsh]] by [[Edward I]], Shrewsbury's strategic importance declined on the [[Welsh Marches]].<ref name="town"/> By the mid 14th century, the diminished military importance of the walls and towers no longer justified their upkeep, although this tower was remodelled (to its final size) during the reign of [[Henry IV of England|Henry IV]]. By the 15th century, wooden houses were being built behind and on the wall by townspeople. Some sections behind Pride Hill and Castle Street were demolished. The stone was reused in town house foundations. By 1580, the tower had become known as Waring's Tower after the Waring family who leased it from the town corporation. It was later called Wingfield's Tower after another occupant.<ref name="town"/>

Throughout the late 18th century the remaining parts of Shrewsbury town walls were demolished and the gateways removed. The Town Walls Tower survived because it remained in use. In 1816 the tower was the workshop of a watch maker named John Massey. In the 1860s, it was converted into a dwelling for the coachmen of John Humphreys, who lived opposite the tower in Swan Hill Court.  His daughter Rachel Humphreys donated the tower to the National Trust in 1930. Between 1930 and 1937 her gardener and his wife lived in the tower. From 1937 to 1954 it was occupied by Mrs. Janet Mitchell. From 1954 to 1967 it was occupied by Mrs. B Curtis. From 1968 to 2012 it was leased by Mr and Mrs Hector. It is now leased by [[Shrewsbury High School, Shropshire|Shrewsbury High School]] and conserved by the [[National Trust]], which uses the tower as a holiday let<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/holidays/shropshire-staffordshire/town-walls-tower|title=Shrewsbury, Shropshire: Town Walls Tower|website=www.nationaltrust.org.uk|accessdate=22 April 2024|archive-date=22 April 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240422222210/https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/holidays/shropshire-staffordshire/town-walls-tower|url-status=live}}</ref> although the tower continues to be open to the public for pre-booked guided tours at least three weekends a year.<ref>{{cite web |title=Visiting Town Walls Tower |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/shropshire-staffordshire/attingham-park-estate-town-walls-tower/visiting-town-walls-tower |website=National Trust |access-date=13 January 2025}}</ref>
